\begin{figure}[H]
  \captionsetup{font=footnotesize}  % 10 pt caption (footnotesize at 12 pt base)
    \vspace{-6mm}   % moves the caption up; adjust to taste
  \caption{\textbf{Patch-leaving behavior is consistent with a Bayesian formulation of the Marginal Value Theorem.}
    (\subref{fig:2-a}) MVT predicts that optimal patch leaving is set by the global reward rate (slope of black tangent lines), and foragers should leave high or low value odor patch types (orange and green lines) at the same local reward rate. 
    (\subref{fig:2-b}) Reward probability at leaving is matched across patch types, while rewards collected, and number of reward omissions experienced differed significantly, ruling out simpler heuristics such as reward counting or win-stay, lose-switch. Lines are individual mice ($n=24$).
    (\subref{fig:2-c}) Mice have odor-cued expectations about patch quality. Given that the first odor site in a patch was unrewarded, mice were more likely to leave the low value patch (green) than the high (orange)
    (\subref{fig:2-d}) Experiments manipulating travel cost. Mean inter-patch distance was increased or decreased without changing reward probability in patch types.  Compared to control conditions, longer distances led mice to stay in patches longer, leaving at a lower $P(\text{reward})$, while shorter distances had the opposite effect.
    (\subref{fig:2-e},\subref{fig:2-f}) Experiments manipulating global reward rate.  In (\subref{fig:2-e}), reward probability of odor 2 patch type was increased to match those of odor 1, while reward probability of odor 1 patch type was unchanged. This led to a higher global reward rate overall. Relative to control sessions, mice left both patch types earlier, at a higher $P(\text{reward})$ (Left). To achieve this, the number of rewards mice collected in the two patch types changed in opposite directions (Right). (\subref{fig:2-f}) The opposite manipulation, led to mice leaving both patches earlier, at a lower $P(\text{reward})$. These results show that mice use global reward rate to inform local patch leaving decisions, consistent with MVT predictions. 
    (\subref{fig:2-g}) Bayesian MVT model schematic. Upon patch entry, the agent draws from a separate posterior over reward probability $q$ for each odor-cued patch type. Within patches, the posterior is updated after each binary outcome via Bayes' rule with a forgetting parameter $\delta < 1$ that discounts accumulated prior beliefs at each update step. At each odor site, a sample $\tilde{q}$ is drawn from the current posterior; the agent leaves if the local reward rate falls below a running estimate of the global reward rate $\bar{R}$.
    (\subref{fig:2-h}--\subref{fig:2-l}) Bayesian MVT model simulations reproduced mouse behavior in (\subref{fig:2-b}--\subref{fig:2-f}): reward probability at leaving, rewards collected and consecutive reward omissions (\subref{fig:2-h}), probability of leaving after early consecutive omissions (\subref{fig:2-i}, change in $P(\text{reward})$ at leaving with inter-patch distance (\subref{fig:2-j}), and results for higher (\subref{fig:2-q}) and lower (\subref{fig:2-l}) global reward rate environments. The results of these simulations demonstrate that the model captures patch-leaving behavior in steady-state and dynamic environments.
    Significance (paired $t$-tests across subjects): ns, not significant; $^{*}p<0.05$, $^{**}p<0.01$, $^{***}p<0.001$.}
  \label{fig:2}
